power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Author contributions -MO conceived and designed the study, ran the experiments and analyses, and wrote the first draft.
EK and GNN supervised the study.
BSG, AS, YB, AWC, EK and GNN interpreted the results and critically revised the manuscript.
All authors approved the final version.

Use of artificial intelligence -Both Claude Opus 5.5 (via Claude Code) and GPT-6 Astra (through Codex) assisted with analysis and figure code, reference checks and editing under the authors' direction; the authors verified all numbers against the frozen outputs and take responsibility for the content.
Medical artificial intelligence (AI) now writes answers faster than anyone can check them.

In real-world use, health systems are already deploying large language models (LLMs) and AI agents to draft replies to patient messages, write clinical notes from recorded visits and answer clinicians' questions at the point of care (1) (2) (3) (4) (5) (6).
text.formatted: In real-world use, health systems are already deploying large language models (LLMs) and AI agents to draft replies to patient messages, write clinical notes from recorded visits and answer clinicians' questions at the point of care <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(1)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(2)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(4)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(6)</ref>.

text.text: As these systems gain capability and autonomy, their output is growing in scale: one health system logged 2.5 million uses of an AI scribe in its first year (3, 4).
text.formatted: As these systems gain capability and autonomy, their output is growing in scale: one health system logged 2.5 million uses of an AI scribe in its first year <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(3,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">4)</ref>.

text.text: Each of these outputs needs evaluation and monitoring.
Not only is this scale impractical for continuous manual evaluation, but data shows that clinicians who review AI drafts still miss many of the errors in them (7).
text.formatted: Not only is this scale impractical for continuous manual evaluation, but data shows that clinicians who review AI drafts still miss many of the errors in them <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(7)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, more scalable and efficient judge models, and frameworks for collaborative work with physicians, are needed.
LLMs used as automated judges are the main answer so far, and they already run at scale (8) (9) (10).
text.formatted: LLMs used as automated judges are the main answer so far, and they already run at scale <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(8)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(9)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(10)</ref>.

text.text: HealthBench, a widely used benchmark of health conversations, grades each answer with an LLM that checks it against physician-written criteria, called rubric items; on some themes that grader agrees with physicians about as often as physicians agree with each other (11).
text.formatted: HealthBench, a widely used benchmark of health conversations, grades each answer with an LLM that checks it against physician-written criteria, called rubric items; on some themes that grader agrees with physicians about as often as physicians agree with each other <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(11)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the compute, time and cost of judging grow with every answer judged.
The strongest current judges, mostly frontier LLMs, might be costly and slow.

In addition, LLM judges show tendencies to return a different verdict when asked again and to favor longer answers, the answer shown in a particular position and answers from their own model family (12) (13) (14) (15).
text.formatted: In addition, LLM judges show tendencies to return a different verdict when asked again and to favor longer answers, the answer shown in a particular position and answers from their own model family <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(12)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(13)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(14)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(15)</ref>.

text.text: Decision-only models are a recently introduced and much cheaper interface.
Rather than writing text, they return a probability for each option the user specifies (16, 17).
text.formatted: Rather than writing text, they return a probability for each option the user specifies <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17)</ref>.

text.text: Jev, from TypeSafe, is priced at US$0.042 per million input tokens, with no charge for output, and answers in well under a second (16).
text.formatted: Jev, from TypeSafe, is priced at US$0.042 per million input tokens, with no charge for output, and answers in well under a second <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16)</ref>.

text.text: For reference, Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at US$4 per million input tokens and US$20 per million output tokens (18, 19), so a judgment can cost a hundredth as much or less.
text.formatted: For reference, Claude Opus 5.5 is priced at US$4 per million input tokens and US$20 per million output tokens <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19)</ref>, so a judgment can cost a hundredth as much or less.

text.text: Beyond cost, asked whether an answer contains a clinically consequential error, a decision model returns the probability that it does.

That probability makes the judge's uncertainty visible, which a bare written verdict does not (20, 21), and it could enable a health system or a research team to set a cutoff at the false-alarm rate it can afford and send clinicians first to the answers the judge is least sure about (22) (23) (24).
text.formatted: That probability makes the judge's uncertainty visible, which a bare written verdict does not <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">21)</ref>, and it could enable a health system or a research team to set a cutoff at the false-alarm rate it can afford and send clinicians first to the answers the judge is least sure about <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(22)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(23)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(24)</ref>.

text.text: Early studies, including our own, have tested decision models on clinical decisions, medical questions and general judging tasks, with promising but mixed results (25) (26) (27).
text.formatted: Early studies, including our own, have tested decision models on clinical decisions, medical questions and general judging tasks, with promising but mixed results <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(25)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(26)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(27)</ref>.

text.text: Whether they can judge opentext medical answers about as well as clinicians and frontier judges has not been tested.
We tested this in a pre-registered evaluation of TypeSafe Jev 1.13 and compared its performance and agreement with experts with those of current frontier LLMs from different providers.
We also propose a practical workflow, Dial-and-Review, to decide which answers Jev flags and which ones clinicians check first.

We split each benchmark by underlying question, so that no question appeared in more than one part: 15% for development, 20% of the rest for validation, and the remainder, about two-thirds of each benchmark, as the held-out test pool.

Over eight development rounds and about 60,000 model calls, we fixed the judges' questions and prompts, built and tested cheap model teams, and set the cutoffs described below (Supplementary Methods S1).
We pre-registered the test on the Open Science Framework (OSF) on 20 October 2026, fixing the hypotheses, the analysis plan and the cutoffs (Supplementary Methods S3).

We used five published benchmarks with expert labels, each designed or used to test automated judges, giving six judging tasks (Figure 1A; Supplementary Table S1 and Supplementary Figure S1) (5, 11, (28) (29) (30).
text.formatted: We used five published benchmarks with expert labels, each designed or used to test automated judges, giving six judging tasks (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>; Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> and Supplementary Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1</ref>) <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(5,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(28)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(29)</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(30)</ref>.

text.text: Each asks a question a clinician would ask of an AI answer: HealthBench meta-evaluation: does an answer in a health conversation meet a physician-written criterion, such as advising emergency care?
Physicians graded each criterion (20,156 rubric items from 2,504 conversations).
When Rubrics Fail: does an answer contain a clinically consequential error?
Each answer appears in its original form and with one error planted by an LLM, such as a wrong dose, a missed contraindication or an omitted safety step (2,742 answers from 641 questions).
MedVAL: how risky is an AI-written clinical document, such as a radiology impression or a note written from a recorded visit, against its source?
Physicians graded risk on four levels (360 documents).
CounselBench-Eval: how good is an answer to a mental-health question, on scales such as empathy and factual correctness?
Five mental-health professionals rated each answer (276 answers, 1,380 ratings).
CounselBench-Adv: does a reply show a named failure, such as inappropriate medication advice?
Mentalhealth professionals labeled each reply (798 replies).
Real-POCQi: which of two AI answers to a real clinician question is better, on axes such as accuracy and clinical utility?
Physicians chose on each axis (759 comparisons, 3,795 axis ratings).
The test pool held 25,091 units, and identical inputs were judged once.
As their authors request, we never display items from HealthBench Professional (31), which enter through When Rubrics Fail, and we did not modify CounselBench items.
text.formatted: As their authors request, we never display items from HealthBench Professional <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(31)</ref>, which enter through When Rubrics Fail, and we did not modify CounselBench items.

text.text: All benchmarks are public, contain no identifiable patient data and were used within their licenses; no participants were recruited, and institutional review board approval was not required.
All judges received the same case text.

Jev (TypeSafe Jev 1.13, snapshot 1.13-20260917) and OpenAI Decisions, which OpenAI lists as running on GPT-6 Luna, chose among fixed answer options (yes or no, a rating scale, or a preference between two answers) and returned a probability for each (16, 17).
text.formatted: Jev (TypeSafe Jev 1.13, snapshot 1.13-20260917) and OpenAI Decisions, which OpenAI lists as running on GPT-6 Luna, chose among fixed answer options (yes or no, a rating scale, or a preference between two answers) and returned a probability for each <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(16,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17)</ref>.

text.text: For When Rubrics Fail, for example, the question was "Does this answer contain a clinically consequential error, such as an incorrect number, dose, timing threshold, diagnosis, contraindication or instruction, that could change diagnosis or management or cause harm?"
The questions used each benchmark's own wording where it existed and were fixed in the first development round (Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: The questions used each benchmark's own wording where it existed and were fixed in the first development round (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Jev's default reading was its most probable option, so it flagged a problem at a probability of 0.5 or more.

GPT-6 Luna, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 received each benchmark's published judge prompt where one existed (HealthBench, MedVAL and CounselBench-Eval), and otherwise the same question as text, and returned a written verdict that we read with fixed rules.
Luna answered three times at low reasoning effort and the majority counted; Sol and Opus answered once at their default settings.
Unreadable answers and refusals counted as missing (Supplementary Table S20).
text.formatted: Unreadable answers and refusals counted as missing (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S20</ref>).

text.text: Frontier models were tested on a matched subset of 3,614 units, drawn at random before any frontier call.
Head-to-head comparisons used these units for every judge.
We also tested the Hybrid team, the best cheap team from development, which pairs the decision models with a cheap LLM.
It keeps Jev's verdict and adds a second opinion only where development showed a gain.

For instance, on When Rubrics Fail a flag from Jev stands only if deleting one passage of the answer lowers Jev's error probability by at least 0.10 and Luna confirms that the passage is wrong (the doublecheck); on MedVAL the team averages Jev's and Decisions' probabilities, and on Real-POCQi it averages Jev's probabilities over both answer orders (Supplementary Table S2).
text.formatted: For instance, on When Rubrics Fail a flag from Jev stands only if deleting one passage of the answer lowers Jev's error probability by at least 0.10 and Luna confirms that the passage is wrong (the doublecheck); on MedVAL the team averages Jev's and Decisions' probabilities, and on Real-POCQi it averages Jev's probabilities over both answer orders (Supplementary Table <ref type="table">S2</ref>).

text.text: Five further team designs from development were tested as pre-registered (Supplementary Methods S2).

The main outcome was plain agreement with the expert label, in percent: agreement with each of the first two physicians on HealthBench, a rating within half a point of the raters' mean on CounselBench-Eval, the same direction of preference on Real-POCQi, and right calls on the other three tasks (Supplementary Methods S4).
Where a second expert rating existed (HealthBench, CounselBench-Eval and Real-POCQi), agreement between experts serves as context.
Because plain agreement rewards a judge for answering with the most common label, we added after scoring the best constant answer, the single answer that maximizes agreement on each task.
The pre-registered comparisons used each benchmark's own measure (Table 2).
text.formatted: The pre-registered comparisons used each benchmark's own measure (Table <ref type="table">2</ref>).

The proposed clinician review then goes first to the passed answers closest to the cutoff, at budgets of 1%, 2% and 5% of answers, compared with a random audit of the same size; on the other tasks, review goes to the units where Jev is least sure.

text.text: In this pre-registered evaluation, a decision-only model that costs a small fraction of current frontier LLMs showed non-inferior to better performance as a clinical judge compared with Opus and Sol, two frontier LLMs costing 34 to 152 times more, on most tasks.

For instance, on HealthBench rubric grading, its agreement with physicians was only 8 points below physicians' agreement with each other, and on physicians' preferences and counseling ratings it was numerically close to the expert reference.

Beyond a fraction of the cost, it worked in a fraction of the time, and it gave a view into its own decisions: a probability for every call, where an LLM judge returns a verdict and an explanation without a usable measure of how sure it is.
We therefore see this as a potential practical proof of concept for the scalable use of decision models to automate the evaluation and monitoring of LLMs, in research and in real-world deployment.

At the costs and speeds measured on the matched subset, one million judgments would cost about US$62 with Jev and take about 11 hours at eight parallel requests, against about US$2,100 and 8 days with Sol, and US$9,400 with Opus at batch prices.
At that price, a health system could score every answer of a deployed assistant rather than a sample, and rerun a fixed set of cases after each model update to see whether anything got worse.

Because Jev is used off the shelf through a hosted interface, a health system could run such monitoring itself, with no model training and no local hardware, unlike fine-tuned judges such as MedVAL-4B and PrecepTron, which need labeled cases for training (29, 32).

text.text: Of course, this is a proposed framework, and it does need agreements for sending patient data to the provider, which we did not examine.

For context, the HealthBench authors report a macro-F1 of 0.57 to 0.73 between physicians by theme and 0.709 for their GPT-4.1 grader, whose prompt was developed on these data; Jev's balanced F1 on our full pool was 0.651, on a different sample and aggregation (11).

text.text: Decision models can also work alongside LLMs rather than replace them: in our earlier study, pairing a decision model with an LLM made clinical decisions less sensitive to framing (25), and on general benchmarks Jev has worked as a first-pass judge that hands hard cases to a larger model (26).

text.text: Here, pairing Jev with a cheap, fast LLM such as Luna gave a lever for settings where false alarms are costly: the Hybrid team's double-check nearly halved false alarms, although moving Jev's own cutoff did as well while missing fewer errors.

A cascade may do better, with Jev screening every answer and passing only the uncertain ones to a frontier LLM, which caught 8.8 points more planted errors than Jev at the same false-alarm rate, or to a clinician.

Still, this can be considered only early, exploratory evidence and should be evaluated for real-world value and with different possible workflows; nonetheless, it opens the space for scalable, cheap and efficient workflows for these types of tasks.

In addition, we see that this might offer insights for work on selective prediction and deferral, which routes uncertain cases to clinicians and confident ones to automation, including in medicine (22) (23) (24); a decision model supplies that signal for the cost of one cheap call.

text.text: Whether such routing improves the care patients receive has to be tested prospectively.

Cutoffs from small development samples drifted, and dials set on 250 answers varied between samples, so a health system should set its dial on its own labeled answers and recheck it over time (34, 35).

text.text: At a practical cutoff, Jev missed about half of planted errors, and some, such as a confident false reassurance, passed Jev, Sol and Opus alike.
Jev is therefore best used to decide where scarce clinician attention goes, with random expert review of passed answers to estimate what every judge misses.
Judges also bring preferences of their own: every judge flagged long correct answers more often, so an update that writes longer answers could look like a safety regression.

In exploratory analysis, the three judges from OpenAI's model family ranked GPT-5.5 first among four answering systems, while physicians ranked it last, as the benchmark's authors also found for GPT-5.5 as a judge (5).

Comparisons across systems or over time should therefore check for answer length and for the judge's model family, and pairwise comparisons should score both answer orders and average them, at the cost of a second call.

Although the performance overall was promising, Jev detected missed contraindications and treatment errors far more often than omissions or failures to seek information, and Opus did little better on omissions, as other studies of LLM judges have found (36, 37).

text.text: One possibility, which we did not test, is that a clinician grading an answer holds a picture of what it should contain, whereas a judge asked a yes-or-no question weighs mainly what the answer says.
We also think the benchmarks carry a lesson for evaluating judges.

On HealthBench, always answering "met" agreed with a physician 77.2% of the time, and plain agreement can rank judges by how often they say yes, a gap between raw and chance-corrected agreement that large evaluations of LLM judges have also found (38).

text.text: Like any study, this one has many limitations.
The test was kept apart from development but drawn from the same five benchmarks, so it is not a proper external validation.

Planted errors may also be cleaner than errors in real answers, and their high prevalence might inflate the absolute yield of review; both the yield and the advantage of ordered review may change in another setting.
Three of six tasks had no second expert rating, and the references that exist were not always built the same way as the judges' scores.
The best constant answers, the six-task averages and the wholepool cost and time were added after scoring, and Sol's and Opus's whole-pool figures are extrapolated from the matched subset.

Overall, a decision-only model judged medical AI answers about as well as frontier LLM judges on most tasks, at a cost and speed that make checking every answer feasible, and its probabilities showed where clinicians might need to look first.

We see this as a practical proof of concept for health systems and developers to adopt not only automated judges but also the wider continuous monitoring and evaluation of automated AI systems, in the real world and at scale.
